line_texts: Layered hybrid perovskites combine strong excitonic binding with a tunable organic spacer. In-plane
transport is described by a diffusion coefficient D_{\parallel} , whereas hopping across
the spacer layers is orders of magnitude slower. Scripts and raw traces are available at example.org/tr-2026-17 .
Here we summarise the measurements and the model used to extract the anisotropy.

line_texts: Samples were prepared by spin coating from a precursor solution and annealed at 100 degrees for ten
minutes. Time-resolved photoluminescence was recorded with a streak camera at several excitation
fluences between 0.1 and 20 microjoules per square centimetre. The exciton density follows a
rate equation with linear decay and bimolecular annihilation, solved here in the low-density limit.
Fits were repeated for three samples of each spacer length and the scatter between samples is
reported as the uncertainty on every extracted parameter in the tables of Section 3.

line_texts: The low-density limit is justified because the annihilation rate is below ten percent of the linear
decay rate for all fluences used in the diffusion measurements. Spatial profiles were obtained by
imaging the emission through a slit and fitting Gaussian widths versus time delay.
The extracted widths grow linearly in time, as expected for ordinary diffusion in two dimensions.
Deviations at short delay are attributed to the finite resolution of the optical setup.

line_texts: Out-of-plane transport is probed by exciting through the substrate and detecting from the top surface.
The arrival time of the front gives the effective perpendicular diffusion constant directly.
Because the barrier layers are thin, tunnelling between neighbouring wells dominates the process.
The anisotropy ratio is therefore very large and depends strongly on the length of the spacer.
The smallest spacer yields the fastest perpendicular transport and the weakest confinement.

exciton line, with a width determined by the binding energy E_{b} of the quantum well.
